findings.source_passage: "Not by nature, perhaps, doc. But I'm talking about art." "Art?" "Why, yes. What's the difficulty? Hire a liner——" "A liner!" murmured Dr. Hall faintly.
findings.source_locator: Julius's 'art' speech, after doctor says conditions cannot repeat
findings.why_it_matters: The full exchange — 'Art?', Julius's deadpan 'Why, yes. What's the difficulty? Hire a liner——', Dr. Hall's faint echo 'A liner!' — is a rhythmically distinctive comic beat. The draft collapses it to 'I'm talking about art. In a few hard phrases he sketched…', erasing the call-and-response that makes Julius's absurdist confidence funny.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the verbatim exchange: 'Art?' / 'Why, yes. What's the difficulty? Hire a liner——' / '"A liner!" murmured Dr. Hall faintly.' Then proceed with Julius's elaboration.

findings.source_passage: "by the time she's got a life-belt on her, and is being hustled into a boat, with a well-drilled lot of artistes doing the hysterical stunt on deck, why--she ought to be right back where she was in May, 1915. How's that for the bare outline?"
findings.why_it_matters: This is the rhetorical peak of Julius's speech — 'well-drilled lot of artistes doing the hysterical stunt on deck' and 'How's that for the bare outline?' are voice-defining, period-flavored, and characterize Julius's breezy transatlantic confidence. The draft replaces the entire vivid elaboration with the summary 'he sketched hiring ship and passengers, and a panic well drilled for the screen.'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum the life-belt/artistes/hysterical-stunt passage and the closing 'How's that for the bare outline?' — these are signature Julius phrases the compression must not paraphrase away.

findings.source_passage: "No," said Julius, in answer to it, "I'm not crazy. The thing's perfectly possible. It's done every day in the States for the movies. Haven't you seen trains in collision on the screen? What's the difference between buying up a train and buying up a liner?"
findings.source_locator: After Dr. Hall's incredulous look at Julius
findings.why_it_matters: Julius's self-defence — 'I'm not crazy. It's done every day in the States for the movies. Haven't you seen trains in collision on the screen?' — is characterologically distinctive and funny; the trains-vs-liner analogy is the kind of confident American logic the chapter hinges on for its comedy. It is entirely absent in the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert Julius's rebuttal verbatim after the doctor's incredulous look: 'No, I'm not crazy. The thing's perfectly possible…what's the difference between buying up a train and buying up a liner?'

findings.source_passage: "I cannot guarantee a cure," he pointed out. "Perhaps I ought to make that quite clear."
findings.source_locator: Doctor's caveat before Julius's 'trot out Jane'
findings.why_it_matters: The doctor's fussy professional qualification ('Perhaps I ought to make that quite clear') is a small but characteristic voice marker — cautious propriety meeting Julius's breezy confidence. The draft drops the second sentence.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain 'Perhaps I ought to make that quite clear.' — it adds only six words and preserves the tonal contrast.

findings.source_passage: "Very remarkable plan. Very remarkable," he murmured. "The movies--of course! Your American word for the kinema. Very interesting. I fear we are perhaps a little behind the times over here in our methods."
findings.source_locator: Doctor's response after Julius explains movie precedent
findings.why_it_matters: The doctor's bumbling, slightly condescending note — 'your American word for the kinema' and 'I fear we are perhaps a little behind the times' — establishes Edwardian English diffidence against American modernity, a register-defining comic beat. The draft strips it to 'Very remarkable plan. Very remarkable.'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the doctor's full murmur through 'a little behind the times over here in our methods' — it is concise and does important tonal work.

summary: Julius's extended liner-plan speech — the rhetorical and comic centrepiece of the chapter — is compressed to a single flat summary sentence, losing the 'artistes doing the hysterical stunt,' the trains-vs-liner rebuttal, and the doctor's 'kinema' exchange; these three medium-severity losses together trigger regeneration.
